transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2027-05-21 15:00 UTC
- Duration: 42 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Sofia (Redwood CSM); Priya (Meridian VP Product), Liam (Meridian SRE), Anya (Meridian ML Ops), Noah (Infra)

Auto-summary: quick alignment on SLO definitions: TTFT (time to first token) vs TPOT (time per output token / time per token streaming), agreed to p95/p99 targets by payload size tier, Redwood to run benchmarks using Meridian's prompt families, next meeting for infra deep-dive.

[00:00] Maya (AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro — me and ethan and sofia from Redwood. priya, do you want to kick off with what you want out of this POC?
[00:18] Priya (VP Product): yeah thanks. high level — we're building an agent assistant inside our customer portal, lots of short queries (single-turn) mixed with some long summarization jobs. our big questions are around latency SLOs and cost. we need to define TTFT vs TPOT and agree p95/p99 targets so we can commit to SLAs in prod.
[00:36] Ethan (SE): makes sense. when you say short queries, what percent of traffic is short vs medium vs long?
[00:44] Priya: roughly 65% short (<32 tokens out), 25% medium (32-256 tokens), 10% long (>256 tokens) for now — but long jobs are more bursty.
[00:57] Liam (SRE): from infra side we care about concurrency and tail latency. we run on GCP, egress rules are locked down, and we'd probably start with hosted but may lift to dedicated if latency or data isolation needs it.
[01:12] Maya: ok good, so there's three axes we usually scope: TTFT (time to first token), TPOT (time per token / tokens per second streaming), and throughput measured as concurrent requests and effective qps. i want to make sure we all have the same defs.
[01:25] Priya: yes please define them; different people use different terms.
[01:29] Ethan: quick defs — TTFT is the latency from request arrival to the first token emitted by the model; TPOT (we also call it time-per-output-token) is the incremental time for each subsequent token, typically influenced by model size, quantization, and CPU/GPU kernel perf. for throughput we look at p95/p99 of completed request latencies and tokens/sec aggregated.
[01:52] Anya (ML Ops): ok that matches our internal thinking. what numbers are realistic? we need p95 for short queries to be <150ms ideally, p99 under 300ms. is that feasible on 13B?
[02:06] Ethan: yes with Redwood Dedicated and some quantization we can hit TTFT p95 ~120-180ms on 13B for short requests, p99 will be higher, often 250-350ms depending on network and warm cache. TPOT usually is around 10-25ms per token on GPU for that model family; you can lower it with batching and fp16 kernels.
[02:26] Maya: to add, caching matters — prefix KV cache can make repeated prompts much faster. important to know how many unique sessions you have vs repeated patterns.
[02:35] Priya: we have lots of templated prompts, maybe 40% are identical templates with different entities. we can share samples.
[02:42] Noah (Infra): on hosted vs dedicated — what are the typical tradeoffs? we want predictable p99s for customer-facing flows.
[02:50] Ethan: hosted gives the fastest path to test but the p99 variability can be larger because multi-tenancy and routing. Dedicated locks you to reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput, so p99 tails tighten. for p99-sensitive production paths we'd recommend Dedicated or a hybrid routing policy (primary dedicated, fallback hosted).
[03:09] Priya: when you say dedicated, what's the typical qps per GPU?
[03:13] Ethan: depends on model/quantization and sequence length. for a 13B quantized model with average response length ~30 tokens, sustained qps per A100-type GPU could be ~10-20 qps, with batching pushing higher; for concurrency you plan for request parallelism and the instance's effective tokens-per-second. we'll create a sizing table in the benchmark deliverable.
[03:35] Liam: ok good. how should we structure the measurement plan? we want numbers we can present to leadership: TTFT p95/p99 by tier, TPOT median/p95, and cost per 1M tokens.
[03:46] Ethan: propose this measurement plan: Redwood runs 1k-sample synthetic benchmark per prompt family (short/med/long) using your exact prompts and average input sizes. We'll measure: TTFT distribution, TPOT distribution, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and cost estimate. We'll do both hosted endpoints and dedicated config. We'll share raw csv + summary sheet.
[04:10] Priya: sounds good. timeline?
[04:14] Maya: we can run initial benchmarks within 7 days once you share prompts and traffic mix. then 2-week pilot where we route a small percent of real traffic to Redwood's hosted endpoint to validate in prod-ish conditions. after that, decision point on dedicated commit.
[04:27] Anya: for SLOs, can we make SLO buckets? like short (<32 tokens): TTFT p95 <=150ms, p99 <=300ms; medium (32-256): TTFT p95 <=250ms, p99 <=450ms; long: p95 we care less about TTFT but TPOT stability matters. does that align?
[04:47] Ethan: yes that's reasonable. i'd add TPOT targets: short TPOT median <=12ms/token, p95 <=25ms/token; medium TPOT median <=18ms/token, p95 <=35ms/token. again depends on model size and quantization profile.
[05:05] Priya: how do you measure TTFT for streaming vs non-streaming responses? sometimes our client shows first token earlier due to chunking.
[05:12] Ethan: good question. measurement method: for streaming we measure time until first bytes reach the TCP layer at client side if the client test harness supports it; for server-side we measure generation start. we'll run both server-side and client-side latency tests to reconcile differences. include network RTT baseline in the report.
[05:33] Noah: network — we'll need VPC peering or PrivateLink for dedicated; otherwise hosted will traverse internet egress. any firewall constraints?
[05:40] Maya: we can work with your infra to open necessary endpoints; for dedicated we support VPC private connectivity. we'll add infra deep-dive follow-up to map firewall rules.
[05:49] Priya: what about cold-start vs warm cache? we have lots of ephemeral containers; cold starts for large models worry us.
[05:56] Ethan: cold starts are usually measured separately — for Dedicated, cold-start is minimal because model stays resident. hosted can have warm/cold variance. we will include cold-start samples in the benchmark (e.g., after 15m idle).
[06:07] Anya: ok. about evaluation artifacts — will you provide a spreadsheet with all testcases and raw measurements?
[06:12] Maya: yes, deliverable will include raw csv, summary pivot sheet with p50/p95/p99 for TTFT and TPOT per prompt family, GPU util and cost estimate. we'll also document test harness (version, model artifact, quantization flags).
[06:24] Priya: any gotchas on quantization? like accuracy/regression risk?
[06:28] Ethan: quantization (4-bit/8-bit) can change output slightly; Redwood Optimize provides recommended quantization profiles per workload. we'll run QA checks: simple BLEU/ROUGE or task-specific evals to ensure quality within acceptance thresholds you define.
[06:44] Liam: on acceptance criteria — leadership wants a clear pass/fail: if TTFT p95 for short is <=150ms and p99 <=300ms on dedicated, we proceed to committed capacity. otherwise we run a tuning pass.
[06:57] Maya: noted. we'll map acceptance criteria into the POC doc.
[07:01] Priya: can you also include cost per 1M tokens for both hosted and dedicated?
[07:06] Ethan: yes, cost model included. hosted shows per-token bill with some variance; dedicated will show amortized infra cost + support. we'll provide sensitivity analysis for qps ranges.
[07:16] Priya: Great. Any risk items?
[07:19] Sophia (CSM): recording action: data residency and SSO — we'll need security artifacts. Priya mentioned SOC2 requirement earlier.
[07:26] Priya: yes we need SOC2 report and encryption details (KMS).
[07:29] Maya: we'll send security docs (SOC2, ISO, KMS integration note) as part of follow-up.
[07:34] Ethan: last technical note — for p99 tightening, we often recommend mixing bigger GPUs for batched throughput and smaller low-latency instances for hot paths. That hybrid helps meet TTFT strict SLOs and keep cost reasonable.
[07:49] Noah: ok makes sense.
[07:51] Priya: recap next steps?
[07:54] Maya: Redwood: run 1k sample benchmarks for each prompt family and share csv + summary by 2027-05-28. Send security artifacts by 2027-05-24. Schedule infra deep-dive for 2027-05-26.
[08:08] Priya: Meridian: share prompt families and traffic mix by 2027-05-24, provide sample traffic trace if possible.
[08:16] Anya: we'll add acceptance criteria to the POC doc and review after results.
[08:21] Ethan: i'll include measurement method: server-side timestamps, client-side first-byte measurement, warm vs cold, batch sizes, concurrency sweep (1, 5, 10, 20), and model variants (13B fp16, 13B 4-bit q, 7B options).
[08:40] Maya: perfect. any other Qs?
[08:43] Liam: just firewall details, we'll compile and send.
[08:46] Maya: great. thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email with the POC plan and links to the benchmark artifact.
[08:53] Priya: thanks all.

End of transcript.

Notes: transcription includes minor speaker label errors in places; timings are approximate. Shared artifacts mentioned during call: "Meridian prompt set (link)" (to be provided by Meridian), "Redwood benchmark csv and summary" (to be delivered), security pack link (Redwood SOC2/ISO).
